ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Eight $1\times 1$ square tiles are arranged as shown so their outside edges form a polygon with a perimeter of $14$ units. Two additional tiles of the same size are added to the figure so that at least one side of each tile is shared with a side of one of the squares in the original figure. Which of the following could be the perimeter of the new figure?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, there are 8 1×1 squares forming a staggered polyomino: the lower row has 4 consecutive squares, the upper row also has 4 consecutive squares, and the upper row as a whole is shifted 1 square to the right relative to the lower row. The problem gives that the perimeter of the original figure is 14. Reasoning: Choose two visible outer positions to add new squares, for example add one below the leftmost square in the lower row, and add one above the rightmost square in the upper row. Each newly added square shares exactly 1 side with the original figure, and these two newly added squares are not adjacent to each other. An isolated 1×1 square has 4 sides; when it shares 1 side with the original figure, this shared side is no longer counted in the outer perimeter, and the corresponding side of the original figure also disappears from the outer boundary, so the net increase in perimeter is 4−2=2. Two such squares together increase the perimeter by 2+2=4. Therefore one possible perimeter of the new figure is 14+4=18.

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram as a staggered 8-square polyomino: four unit squares in the lower row and four in the upper row, with the upper row shifted one square to the right. Use the text-given initial perimeter 14. Choose two exterior attachment spots visible in the diagram where a new tile would touch the original figure along exactly one side and would not touch the other new tile, for example one below the lower-left square and one above the upper-right square. Each such added unit square contributes 4 new edges but removes the 1 shared original edge from the boundary and also has its matching edge hidden, so the net perimeter change is +2 per tile. Therefore the new perimeter can be 14 + 2 + 2 = 18 units.

method.method_draft: Model the image on a square grid: original squares occupy lower-row columns 1 through 4 and upper-row columns 2 through 5. Add two valid squares, for instance at lower-row column 1's underside and upper-row column 5's top side. Then count perimeter globally with the formula P = 4N - 2A, where N is the number of unit squares and A is the number of shared sides between pairs of squares. From the diagram, the original 8-tile figure has 9 shared sides total, consistent with perimeter 4(8)-2(9)=14. The two added tiles each introduce exactly one new shared side with the original and no shared side with each other, so after adding them N=10 and A=11. Thus P=4(10)-2(11)=40-22=18 units.
